blocks.title: Translation moment: 'I want to know if my SIP increase actually helped'

steps.label: Day 0 — Baseline
steps.body: Take all 3 measurements. Net worth ₹4.2L, savings rate 12%, burn ₹85K. Don't read too hard yet — single points are noise.

steps.label: Day 1 — Single intervention
steps.body: Increase SIP by ₹10K/month. Don't change anything else. Single variable.

steps.label: Day 7 — Mid-check
steps.body: Take all 3 measurements again. Notice any drift in spending — are you compensating for the SIP by cutting something else, or by sliding into credit?

steps.label: Day 14 — Final check
steps.body: Final measurement. Net worth +₹15K (SIP impact + market drift). Savings rate 18% (up 6 points). Burn ₹84K (basically unchanged — good).

steps.label: Day 15 — Decide
steps.body: Keep, modify, or drop. Here: keep. The SIP increase didn't trigger compensatory spending. Lock in. Set a calendar reminder for the next experiment.

blocks.prompt: Why is *savings rate* a more useful weekly metric than *total saved this month*?

choices.label: It's normalized to income — comparable across pay raises and pay cuts
choices.explain: Correct. ₹10K saved on a ₹50K salary is very different from ₹10K saved on a ₹2L salary. Rate captures this.

choices.label: It's easier to calculate
choices.explain: Both require the same two numbers; the rate just divides them.

choices.label: Banks reward you for high savings rate
choices.explain: Not in any direct way.

choices.label: It hides the absolute amount, which is private
choices.explain: Not the reason; both are personal data.

coach.name: RBI Rohan
coach.role: Used to work at RBI; reads household-finance data for fun

intro: Remember: a real effect shows in 2 of 3 numbers, not just the one you wanted to move.

scenarios.situation: Switch from regular-plan to direct-plan funds. Net worth +₹12K (market drift), savings rate unchanged 14%, burn unchanged ₹78K.
scenarios.explain: Free upgrade. Net worth gain matches the 0.85% saving applied to corpus. Zero behavioral cost. Lock in.

scenarios.situation: Increase SIP by ₹15K/month. Net worth -₹3K (market drift), savings rate 25% (up 8), burn ₹95K (UP from ₹85K — credit card balance grew).
scenarios.explain: Bug! The SIP increase caused compensatory spending on credit. Net effect is negative — you're saving more in the equity column but accumulating debt at 36%. Modify: roll back ₹5K of the SIP increase, monitor burn.

scenarios.situation: Cut subscriptions and dining out. Net worth +₹8K, savings rate 19% (up 7), burn ₹73K (down from ₹85K).
scenarios.explain: All three numbers moved positively. Strong signal. Keep, then run the next experiment.

scenarios.situation: Move emergency fund from savings A/C (4%) to liquid fund (7%). Net worth +₹1K, savings rate unchanged, burn unchanged.
scenarios.explain: Tiny positive on net worth from the rate differential; zero behavioral cost. Free win, even if it's small in absolute terms.

scenarios.situation: Try a strict ₹15K/week food budget. Net worth +₹2K, savings rate 16% (up 2), burn ₹80K (down 5K), but: 'I'm exhausted, this isn't sustainable'.
scenarios.explain: Worked in numbers, failed in sustainability. The note matters as much as the data. Modify: relax the budget to ₹18K/week, find the level you can hold without burning out.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the dashboard delusion
blocks.md:
Saturday night. Excited. You build a 22-widget Notion dashboard with mood emoji column, automated graphs, savings-rate sparklines, currency conversion, color-coded categories, custom Hindi labels. Bahut santosh.

Monday: glanced once.

Wednesday: 'I'll update it on the weekend.' Didn't.

Friday: forgot the link.

Month later: dashboard is dead. The 3-number plain-text note you almost dismissed would still be running.

**Three numbers. Plain text. Sunday 9 pm. Anything fancier is procrastination wearing the costume of productivity.**

Tracking is necessary, not sufficient. The experiment is: pick ONE intervention, run for 14 days, compare baseline to final.

Good single-variable interventions:
- Switch one fund to direct-plan equivalent
- Increase SIP by a specific ₹ amount
- Cap one spending category (dining, subscriptions, ride-share)
- Open and start a liquid-fund SIP
- Surrender a non-performing product

The rule for reading results: **a real effect shows in 2 of 3 numbers, not just the one you hoped would move.** If only savings rate goes up but burn also goes up (because credit-card debt grew), the intervention has a hidden cost.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps in a clean 14-day money experiment:

items.label: Pick ONE intervention; ignore the other three you wanted to try
items.detail: Single-variable discipline.

items.label: Take baseline measurements on Day 0 (Sunday)
items.detail: Without baseline, the after-numbers are unreadable.

items.label: Run the intervention for 14 uninterrupted days; resist tweaking mid-flight
items.detail: Drift effects need 2 weeks to settle out of noise.

items.label: Compare Day 0 vs Day 14 across ALL 3 numbers, not just the favorite
items.detail: Cherry-picking the metric that moved is the most common bug.

items.label: Decide: keep / modify / drop / inconclusive — and record the decision in writing
items.detail: Decisions in your head don't count; the journal is the system.

blocks.instruction: Design YOUR first 14-day money experiment. Specify: (a) the single intervention, (b) Day 0 baseline date, (c) Day 7 mid-check date, (d) Day 14 final date, (e) success criterion in numeric terms.
blocks.expected:
Example:
(a) Intervention: Switch ₹3L from regular-plan active fund to direct-plan Nifty 50 index fund.
(b) Baseline: this Sunday 9 pm — note net worth, savings rate, burn.
(c) Mid-check: next Sunday 9 pm — confirm switch processed; note any market drift.
(d) Final: Sunday after that, 9 pm.
(e) Success: net worth flat or up (rate differential too small to dominate market noise in 2 weeks); savings rate unchanged; burn unchanged. The real benefit is over decades; the experiment confirms zero behavioral cost. Decision: keep.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about the 14-day money experiment loop:

choices.label: A real effect shows up in 2 of 3 numbers — favoring the metric you hoped would move and ignoring the others is the most common bug
choices.explain: Correct. The rule is design discipline — it forces you to confront tradeoffs (e.g. SIP up but burn also up means hidden debt growing).

choices.label: Inconclusive is a valid outcome — it means run another 14 days, not panic
choices.explain: Correct. Some interventions need a longer window to read past noise.

choices.label: Multiple interventions at once is more efficient than one at a time
choices.explain: False. With multiple changes you can't tell which moved the numbers; the experiment is uninterpretable.

choices.label: Tracking weekly for a month gives the same information as a single-variable 14-day experiment
choices.explain: False. Tracking shows drift; experiments show causation. Different jobs.

hi-IN.title: Bhabhi-ji ka audit method — every diwali
hi-IN.md:
Indian household har Diwali pe ek annual review hota hai. *Yeh saal hum ne kya kharcha kara, kya saved? Next saal ka plan?*

Yeh exactly same hai but at a smaller scale. **Diwali audit, scaled to weekly.** 14-day experiment. Tracking 3 numbers.

Mummy ne kabhi PowerPoint nahi banayi. Ek register, paanch entries, decision. Same outcome. Better discipline.

**Tu ye system 25 saal pehle ghar pe dekha tha. Use kar.**

en.title: The annual-Diwali-audit, weekly
en.md: Most Indian households run an informal annual review each Diwali — what worked, what didn't, what's next year's plan. The 14-day experiment is the same loop, scaled up. The discipline existed in your home; what's missing is the cadence.

blocks.title: Where you are now
blocks.md:
Five lessons in. You walked in with one diffuse anxiety about money. You're walking out with: a model (income vs spending vs net worth), four named traps (lifestyle inflation, LIC-aunty trap, the active-fund fee drag, the dashboard delusion), two cheat codes (emergency fund + index investing), and a 14-day experimental loop with 3 numbers.

**That's a complete system. Ship it.**

blocks.title: Field Notes: The ₹18K Subscription Leak Nobody Noticed
blocks.source: DINK couple in Gurgaon (mid-30s, both in product roles at large tech firms), audit shared anonymously after a Falguni reader workshop
blocks.story:
In November 2025 a 34/35 couple ran the **14-day burn audit** I prescribe at every workshop. Both earn well, both consider themselves 'careful with money', no expensive vices. They expected to find maybe ₹2-3K of leaks. They wanted to feel virtuous.

For 14 days they logged every rupee out — UPI, card, cash, auto-debit, EMI, the lot — into a single Notion table, with a single column called *recurring?*. No judgement, no categorisation theatre, just a list.

The audit surfaced **₹18,140/month in pure subscription leakage** they had no idea about:

- Netflix (his) + Netflix (hers, different profile, both billing): **₹1,498**
- Two overlapping music subscriptions (Spotify + Apple Music): **₹318**
- Three news subscriptions, one of which had auto-renewed at full ₹6,999/yr: **₹583/mo amortised**
- A ₹2,400/mo gym membership last used in March 2024: **₹2,400**
- ChatGPT Plus + Claude Pro + Perplexity Pro (all 'for work', none reimbursed): **₹4,890**
- iCloud 2TB (her) + Google One 2TB (him), both ~40% empty: **₹1,490**
- A ₹999/mo meditation app last opened 11 months ago: **₹999**
- An expired domain auto-renewing on the wife's old freelance card: **₹4,200/yr → ₹350/mo**
- A wine club shipping monthly that they'd been re-gifting unopened: **₹2,499**
- 8 different Patreon/Substack subs: **₹2,113**

Total: **₹18,140/month = ₹2.18L/year.** At 12% compounded for 25 years: **~₹3.4 crore of foregone wealth, paid in monthly instalments to forgotten free trials.**

They cancelled 80% of it the same evening. The remaining 20% they re-subscribed deliberately, with end dates.
blocks.takeaway: You cannot optimise a budget you have not seen. The 14-day audit is not about discipline — it's about **visibility**. The leakage is always larger than you think and almost always in your blind spot.

blocks.title: Aarav's 14-Day Experiment
blocks.setup:
Last call with Aarav before the wedding. He is 31, three weeks into being a Staff engineer. He has done the work — the SIP is at ₹80K, the EF is built, the ULIP was surrendered, the inheritance is allocated. He is, on paper, sorted.

But he tells you, slightly sheepish: *'Falguni — I want to do something concrete in the next two weeks before Meera and I get into wedding chaos. I have three things on my list:*

1. *Set up the **SIP step-up plan** — automate a 10% increase every January.*
2. *Top up the EF cushion in case the wedding overruns.*
3. *Audit the surrendered-ULIP investment to make sure the index allocation actually went through.*

*I have ~10 hours of focus over the next 14 days. Pick ONE for me, please.'*

This is the final stage. Pick the right one and tell him *why*.

coach.name: FIRE-walla Falguni
coach.role: Ex-Deutsche Bank, retired at 41, runs a personal-finance Substack from Goa

stages.prompt: Which of his three should you actually pick — and is there a fourth, more important option he hasn't named?

options.label: Set up the SIP step-up. It's the highest-leverage action — 10% step-up over 30 years adds ~₹2 cr to terminal wealth. Do it once, automate forever.
options.explain: It is high-leverage and you should absolutely do it — but **it takes 8 minutes, not 10 hours**. Most AMC apps have a one-tap step-up option. Picking this as the 'big project' wastes 9.8 hours on something that's already solved. Wrong shape of task for the time available.

options.label: Top up the emergency fund. Wedding is 11 months out, better safe than sorry.
options.explain: EF is at the **target ₹8.4L** already. Adding more before the wedding is *anxiety expressed as money*. Above-target EF is dead capital — additional rupees here are earning 6.5% pre-tax instead of compounding in equity. The right move when you feel anxious is rarely to add to the cushion; it's usually to *understand the burn*.

options.label: Audit the ULIP-proceeds redeployment. Check the cheque cleared, the STP was set up, the right fund was selected.
options.explain: Important, but it's a 30-minute due-diligence task — open Coin, verify the SIP mandate, screenshot it, done. Doesn't fit the '10 hours over 14 days' budget either.

options.label: **None of the three. Run a 14-day burn audit.** Log every outflow for 14 days into a single sheet with a *recurring?* column. The other three are 30-min admin tasks; the audit is the only one that returns Aarav information he doesn't already have, and it's the only one that informs every future decision.
options.explain: This is the answer. The three things on his list are **already-known knowns** — they need a few minutes of admin, not 10 hours of focus. The unknown — **his actual burn pattern, leak profile, and pre-marriage baseline** — is the only thing that genuinely requires the time he has. And he needs the baseline now so that married-Aarav has a *before* number to compare against. Run the audit.

stages.prompt:
Aarav is convinced. He's never done a burn audit. He asks: *'What's the cheapest way to do this — am I downloading some app, paying for Walnut Plus, building a Notion thing? Don't tell me to manually log everything, I won't last 3 days.'*

Design the actual mechanism:

options.label: Download a fancy aggregator app (Walnut, Money View, Cred Track). Let it auto-categorise from SMS. Look at the report on day 14.
options.explain: Two failure modes. (1) **SMS-scraping aggregators miss UPI, miss split bills, mis-categorise 30% of transactions.** (2) Watching a passive dashboard doesn't change behaviour. The **act of logging it yourself** is what creates the behaviour change — the dashboard view is downstream of that.

options.label: **One Notion table. 4 columns: date, amount, what, *recurring? Y/N*.** Manual entry, but only takes 90 seconds at end of each day. The discipline of typing it is the point. On day 14, sort by *recurring=Y* and decide for each line: keep, kill, downgrade.
options.explain: Correct. The *recurring?* column is the killer feature — it surfaces the leak class (subscriptions, EMIs, auto-debits) separately from one-off spending. 90 seconds × 14 days = 21 minutes total of logging. The *decisions* on day 14 are where the 10 hours actually go. Cheap, manual, behaviour-changing, and the audit becomes a quarterly habit.

options.label: Just download the bank statement on day 15 and analyse it then. No need to log daily.
options.explain: Misses the behavioural mechanism entirely. A bank statement reviewed *after the fact* tells you what happened; daily logging changes what happens next. The act of typing 'Zomato — ₹487' on Tuesday quietly stops the Wednesday Zomato. Statements are forensics; logging is therapy.

options.label: Use both — aggregator for one-time spending, manual for subscriptions.
options.explain: Two systems = no system. The whole point is one source of truth, low friction, decision-forcing. Aarav will abandon both within 5 days. Pick one, the manual one, and execute it cleanly.

stages.prompt:
Day 15 arrives. Aarav has logged 87 transactions across 14 days. He sorts by *recurring? = Y* and finds **₹11,200/month of subscriptions and auto-debits** he didn't realise were active. Smaller than the Gurgaon couple's ₹18K, but real.

What does he *do* with that information today, before the energy fades?

options.label: Cancel everything aggressive — all 11K, redirect entirely to the SIP step-up. Maximum optimisation.
options.explain: Two problems. (1) Some of those subscriptions are genuinely valuable — cancelling all of them is austerity theatre, and austerity always reverses with interest. (2) The behavioural lift is the wrong shape — if Aarav cancels 11 things in one evening he resubscribes to 6 of them within a month from sheer reflex. **Decide each one deliberately.**

options.label: **Three buckets in one sitting: KILL (cancel today), DOWNGRADE (move to cheaper tier or annual billing), KEEP-WITH-DATE (set a calendar reminder to re-decide in 90 days).** Whatever monthly amount that frees up — automate it as a SIP top-up the same evening so the savings *cannot* re-leak into lifestyle.
options.explain: Exactly. The KILL/DOWNGRADE/KEEP-WITH-DATE frame forces a decision per line item without nuking everything. The **automate-the-saving-the-same-evening** bit is the load-bearing rule — every rupee of leak that gets surfaced and *not* re-routed into a SIP within 24 hours will silently become a Swiggy order or a different subscription within 30 days. Money flows to the path of least friction; you have to lay the rail.

options.label: Show the spreadsheet to Meera. Make this a joint decision — joint money habits start now.
options.explain: Good instinct, wrong sequence. Meera's audit is *her* audit; bringing her into Aarav's first-ever audit on day 15, while she is in wedding-planning mode, will turn a productive personal exercise into a relationship debate about whose Netflix gets cancelled. Do this as a **couple's quarterly audit** post-wedding — that's a different ritual. Right now, Aarav decides on his own line items, automates his own savings.

options.label: Cancel only the obvious zombies (gym not used, expired domain). Leave the active subscriptions alone — they're 'reasonable'.
options.explain: This is how the Gurgaon couple ended up with ₹18K of leakage in the first place — every individual subscription was 'reasonable'. The leak is in **the cumulative**, not the individual. Force a decision on every line item, including the reasonable ones. The two Netflix accounts both feel reasonable; together they aren't.

stages.prompt:
Final question. Aarav has run the audit, made the decisions, redirected ₹7,800/month of recovered leakage into his SIP (now ₹87,800/month). He asks: *'Falguni — when do I do this again? Once a year? Once a quarter? Or never, because I've now built the habit?'*

Close the loop.

options.label: Once a year, in January with your tax filing. Keeps it linked to a habit that already exists.
options.explain: Once-a-year is too rare — subscriptions creep, lifestyle inflates, life events change the burn shape. By the next January, 6-9 months of leakage has compounded. Tying it to tax filing also bundles it with a stressful task; it gets skipped in busy years.

options.label: **Quarterly, 14 days each — and *always* immediately after a major life event (wedding, new job, baby, parent moves in).** Life-event audits matter most because the burn-shape is structurally different on the other side. Quarterly keeps the muscle warm; life-event audits prevent silent drift.
options.explain: This is the durable answer. Quarterly is frequent enough to catch creep, infrequent enough not to become a chore. Life-event triggers are the single highest-leverage moment to re-audit because **every assumption in the previous burn baseline just changed**. Married-Aarav, new-dad-Aarav, sabbatical-Aarav each need a fresh audit. The plan that worked at 31 will quietly fail at 34 if no one re-checks.

options.label: Never again — the habit is built, the subscriptions are clean. Auditing is a one-time setup.
options.explain: Subscriptions don't stay clean. New ones get added (work tools, kid apps, family plans), old ones change pricing, free trials convert. The Gurgaon couple in the field notes had run an audit two years prior — and still found ₹18K of leakage on the second one. The audit is a recurring instrument, not a one-off cleanup.

outcomes.perfect: Aarav now has a SIP at ₹87,800/month (after recovered leakage), a quarterly audit ritual, and a framework that survives wedding, kids, and the inevitable Staff-to-Principal promotion. He just bought his future self decades of compounding paid for entirely by killed subscriptions. This is the finale — and the only sustainable finale — of personal finance.
outcomes.good: Aarav ran the audit, killed the obvious zombies, redirected ~₹4-5K to the SIP. He'll do this once more in 2026 and then drift. Still meaningfully better off than 90% of his cohort.
outcomes.learn: Aarav set up the step-up SIP in 8 minutes and spent the other 9 hours 52 minutes scrolling Reddit. He never ran the audit. In 2027, he'll look at his bank statement and find ₹14K/month of leakage he doesn't recognise. Re-read the Gurgaon field notes — visibility is the only intervention that scales.

points: Three numbers — net worth, savings rate, monthly burn — are enough; more is procrastination
Savings rate is normalized to income; comparable across raises and cuts
One intervention, 14 days, before-after; that's the loop
A real effect shows in 2 of 3 numbers — favoring the favorite is the most common bug
Inconclusive is a valid outcome — run another 14 days, don't panic

assessment.title: Money Fundamentals Assessment
assessment.description: Tests whether you can spot the named traps, run the math on Indian retail products, and design a measurable financial experiment that survives contact with a LIC Aunty pitch.

questions.stem: Vikram, 27, just got a 25% raise. Most defensible first move?

choices.label: Increase his automated SIP by an amount close to the raise BEFORE lifestyle adapts
choices.explanation: Correct. Hedonic adaptation works in your favor when the autopay moves the money before you 'notice' the cash.

choices.label: Upgrade his car immediately to celebrate
choices.explanation: Lifestyle inflation textbook. The EMI consumes the raise; net wealth impact ≈ zero.

choices.label: Wait 6 months to 'see the steady state'
choices.explanation: The waiting window is when lifestyle creep happens. Front-load the discipline.

choices.label: Take a personal loan to invest while rates are low
choices.explanation: Leverage on equity is high-variance and unnecessary; the new cashflow is enough.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO statements that match the lifestyle-inflation pattern:

choices.label: Spending tends to scale with income unless you actively design against it
choices.explanation: Correct. Default behavior is to absorb income.

choices.label: Wealth is a function of the GAP between income and spending, compounded
choices.explanation: Correct. Income alone does not determine wealth.

choices.label: Bigger income always means proportionally bigger wealth
choices.explanation: False — exactly the lifestyle-inflation fallacy.

choices.label: Lifestyle inflation only affects people earning over ₹50L
choices.explanation: False — the percentage is similar across brackets; only the absolute numbers change.

questions.stem: How big should the emergency fund be?

choices.label: 6 months of essential expenses (rent, food, utilities, EMIs) — discretionary spending stops in an emergency
choices.explanation: Correct. Sized to what you have to pay, not what you do pay.

choices.label: 6 months of total spending including dining and travel
choices.explanation: Overshoots — discretionary spending can be cut in an actual emergency.

choices.label: Equal to your annual salary
choices.explanation: Way more than needed; over-buffering has opportunity cost.

choices.label: ₹50,000 fixed
choices.explanation: Doesn't scale to your actual costs; useless for someone with ₹65K essential burn.

questions.stem: Where should the emergency fund be parked?

choices.label: Liquid mutual fund or sweep-in FD — accessible in 1-2 days, ~7% return
choices.explanation: Correct. Right balance of accessibility and rate.

choices.label: Equity index fund — best returns long-term
choices.explanation: Wrong shape; the day you need it is often the day equity is down.

choices.label: Credit card limit
choices.explanation: That's debt at 36%, not a buffer.

choices.label: Savings account — instant access
choices.explanation: Inferior to liquid fund — same accessibility, ~3% lower yield.

questions.stem: Using the Rule of 72: at 12% annual return, ₹1 lakh becomes ₹4 lakh in roughly:

choices.label: 12 years (two doubles, 6 years each)
choices.explanation: Correct. 72/12 = 6 years per double; ₹1L → ₹2L → ₹4L.

choices.label: 6 years
choices.explanation: That's one double, ₹1L → ₹2L.

choices.label: 24 years
choices.explanation: Four doubles, ₹1L → ₹16L. Too far.

choices.label: 36 years
choices.explanation: Six doubles, ₹1L → ₹64L.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about compounding:

choices.label: The last decade of any 30-year run does most of the work — hockey-stick shape
choices.explanation: Correct. The last two doubles produce most of the absolute wealth.

choices.label: Time matters more than amount — starting at 25 with ₹10K/month beats starting at 35 with ₹20K/month
choices.explanation: Correct. The extra decade adds ~3x outcome on the same total contribution.

choices.label: Fees do not compound — they're flat charges
choices.explanation: False. Fees compound against you exactly the way returns compound for you.

choices.label: Returns above 15% are sustainable for retail investors over decades
choices.explanation: False. 12-13% nominal is the historical Indian-equity ballpark; assuming 15%+ is overconfident.

questions.stem: Why does most actively-managed Indian large-cap mutual funds underperform the Nifty 50 over 10-year windows?

choices.label: After the 1.5-2% expense ratio, the manager has to beat the index by ~1.5% per year just to break even — almost none can do that consistently
choices.explanation: Correct. The fee math + market efficiency combine to make consistent outperformance very rare.

choices.label: Active fund managers are bad at their jobs
choices.explanation: Misleading. Many are skilled; the issue is the fee math.

choices.label: Indian markets are too small for active management
choices.explanation: Same pattern holds globally; not the primary reason.

choices.label: Index funds use proprietary algorithms
choices.explanation: Index funds just buy whatever's in the index — minimal complexity.

questions.stem: An 'investment' product promises ₹15L back on ₹50K/year × 15 years = ₹7.5L invested. What's the approximate IRR?

choices.label: About 6-7% nominal — roughly zero real return after inflation; classic endowment-LIC math
choices.explanation: Correct. The 'doubles your money in 15 years' framing hides a sub-7% IRR. Same money in a Nifty index would average ~₹26L.

choices.label: About 12% — same as equity
choices.explanation: False; equity at 12% on ₹50K/year for 15 years compounds to ~₹26L, not ₹15L.

choices.label: About 4% — same as savings account
choices.explanation: Slightly low; ~6-7% IRR is the actual.

choices.label: About 10% — beats most mutual funds
choices.explanation: False; the math doesn't support 10%.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO products that should be unbundled from each other:

choices.label: ULIP (Unit-Linked Insurance Plan) — buy term + index separately
choices.explanation: Correct. Bundled high-fee product; both jobs done poorly.

choices.label: Endowment LIC — buy term + index separately
choices.explanation: Correct. Insurance-as-investment with negative real returns.

choices.label: Term insurance + index fund (held separately)
choices.explanation: Not bundled; this IS the recommended setup.

choices.label: PPF + NPS (held separately)
choices.explanation: Both are separate products doing different jobs; both fine to hold.

questions.stem: What's the biggest difference between regular and direct mutual fund plans?

choices.label: Direct plans skip the advisor commission, saving 0.7-1% per year on the same underlying fund
choices.explanation: Correct. Same fund, same returns, no middleman fee.

choices.label: Direct plans have higher minimum investments
choices.explanation: Usually identical or even lower minimums on direct platforms.

choices.label: Direct plans use different stocks
choices.explanation: Same underlying portfolio.

choices.label: Direct plans require a CFP
choices.explanation: Direct plans are SELF-managed; no CFP needed.

questions.stem: Which 3 numbers would you track weekly for personal finance?

choices.label: Net worth, savings rate, monthly burn
choices.explanation: Correct. Score, input rate, output rate. Three numbers cover the system.

choices.label: Net worth, FD interest, gold price
choices.explanation: Mostly noise; doesn't include input or burn.

choices.label: Total income, total spending, credit-card balance
choices.explanation: Two of these are correct (sub-components of burn/savings rate); credit-card balance alone misses the bigger picture.

choices.label: Crypto value, equity value, debt value
choices.explanation: Asset-only view; misses spending and savings rate.

questions.stem: After a 14-day experiment: net worth +₹3K (market drift), savings rate +6 points, burn +₹8K (credit card balance grew). Best interpretation?

choices.label: Modify — the SIP increase caused compensatory spending on credit; roll back partially and monitor burn
choices.explanation: Correct. Only one number truly improved; the other moved the wrong way (debt growing). Hidden cost.

choices.label: Massive success — keep at all costs
choices.explanation: Ignores the burn increase and credit-card growth. Classic cherry-pick.

choices.label: Drop entirely
choices.explanation: Overcorrection; savings rate did improve. The fix is partial rollback, not full abandonment.

choices.label: Inconclusive — do nothing
choices.explanation: Two numbers gave clear signals (one good, one bad); not inconclusive.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about emergency funds:

choices.label: Should be in a liquid fund or sweep-in FD — not equity, not under the mattress
choices.explanation: Correct. Accessibility + rate balance.

choices.label: Sized at 6 months of essential expenses, not 6 months of total spending
choices.explanation: Correct. Discretionary spending stops in emergencies.

choices.label: Once you have an emergency fund, you should immediately put 100% in equity
choices.explanation: False. The buffer should stay liquid; new money goes to equity.

choices.label: Credit-card limits are functionally equivalent to an emergency fund
choices.explanation: False. Cards are 36% debt; not a buffer.

questions.stem: Your friend says 'this 5-star active fund returned 15% last year, switching from index'. Best response?

choices.label: Past performance does not predict future. Rating reflects what HAS happened; the fee will compound against them. Show them the SPIVA report.
choices.explanation: Correct. Most 5-star funds revert to mean over the next 5 years; the fee differential is the persistent damage.

choices.label: Switch immediately to maximize returns
choices.explanation: Performance-chasing; classic retail mistake.

choices.label: Buy a different active fund instead
choices.explanation: Doesn't address the fee math.

choices.label: Add ULIPs for diversification
choices.explanation: ULIPs are exactly what to avoid; doesn't help.

questions.stem: Pick the TWO statements that match the relationship between fees and compounding:

choices.label: A 1.4% annual fee compounds against you, extracting ~30% of your corpus over 30 years
choices.explanation: Correct. Same exponential math as returns, in reverse.

choices.label: Direct-plan funds save 0.7-1% per year compared to regular plans
choices.explanation: Correct. The advisor commission is the differential.

choices.label: Fees only matter for portfolios above ₹1Cr
choices.explanation: False. The percentage damage is identical across portfolio sizes.

choices.label: ULIP fees normalize after year 5 so the early-year damage is recoverable
choices.explanation: False. Early-year compounding is permanent loss; the 'normalization' is too late.

questions.stem: You're paying ₹3,000/month for various subscriptions you barely use. At 12% opportunity cost over 30 years, this leakage costs you approximately:

choices.label: About ₹1 crore
choices.explanation: Correct. ₹3K/month × 30 years × 12% compounding ≈ ₹1Cr. Subscriptions compound.

choices.label: About ₹10 lakh
choices.explanation: Way too low; doesn't account for compounding.

choices.label: About ₹3 lakh
choices.explanation: That's just the principal × 8 years; doesn't account for compounding.

choices.label: Nothing — small amounts don't matter
choices.explanation: Classic 'just ₹150 hai' fallacy.

project.title: Capstone: Build Aanya's 14-Day Money Plan
project.prompt:
Your friend Aanya, 28, slacks you on a Saturday afternoon:

*"Yaar, I have a problem. I just got a ₹40 lakh inheritance from my Naani. ₹18L/year salary, no debt, ₹2L saved in savings A/C, no investments. Living with parents in Pune so my burn is ₹40K/month. The family WhatsApp group has been pitching me products all week — LIC endowment, ULIP, a flat in Hinjewadi. I'm overwhelmed. What do I do?"*

Deliverable, in a single document:

1. **Diagnose** which named traps from this course she's likely facing or about to face. Name them. Cite the lesson.
2. **Propose ONE primary intervention** for the first 14 days (single variable, not three). Justify why this one over the alternatives.
3. **Specify the rewire** for that intervention: cue, friction reduction, tiny first step, accountability — adapted to a money context.
4. **Specify the measurement plan**: which 3 numbers, captured when, success criteria in numeric terms.
5. **Anticipate the failure mode**: name the most likely way the plan derails (family pressure, LIC Aunty, lifestyle creep), and one guardrail.
6. **Sketch the 90-day plan**: what comes after the first 14 days — buffer, then index fund, then PPF, etc. Concrete amounts, ordered.

It should be the kind of plan you'd actually send Aanya at 4 pm Saturday, with the ₹40 lakh sitting in her bank account waiting for a decision.

levels.label: Diagnosis names 3+ specific course traps with correct application; intervention choice is justified against the alternatives (LIC, flat, ULIP); the 90-day plan reflects the lesson order (buffer → debt-free → index → tax-advantaged).
Diagnosis names 1-2 traps; intervention is plausible but lightly justified.
Generic advice; no named traps; no clear reasoning.
Plan is tailored to Aanya's specific situation (28, Pune, parents, ₹40L inheritance, ₹18L income, ₹40K burn, no debt); cue and accountability are realistic for a 28-year-old salaried professional.
Plan is partially adapted; some elements feel generic.
Generic plan that could be sent to anyone; ignores stated context (e.g. ignores the inheritance windfall, or the family-pressure pattern).
All 4 parts of the rewire specified concretely; all 3 measurement numbers and success thresholds stated; failure mode + guardrail named; 90-day plan has specific rupee amounts and dates.
Most parts specified; one or two left vague (e.g. amounts vague, or accountability hand-waved).
Plan reads as advice rather than a runnable 14-day protocol.

credential.title: Money Fundamentals
credential.description: Holder can diagnose common money biases (lifestyle inflation, LIC-aunty trap, fee leakage), distinguish good Indian retail products from bundled bad ones, run 14-day single-variable money experiments, and ship a coherent 90-day financial plan.
